candidate.title: Free Trial Subscription Trap Scam
candidate.summary: Ads lure shoppers with a "risk-free" trial for the cost of shipping only, then quietly enroll them in an expensive recurring subscription that's deliberately hard to cancel. Regulators say this negative-option billing tactic is still actively being used by major companies and is under a renewed wave of FTC and state enforcement.
safetyTips: Read full terms and conditions before entering any payment information for a “free” trial
Set a calendar reminder a few days before the trial period ends to cancel if you don't want to keep paying
Check bank and credit card statements regularly for unrecognized recurring charges
Search the company name online with words like “complaint” or “subscription scam” before signing up
Consider using a virtual or single-use card number for trial offers so unauthorized charges can be blocked
candidate.howItWorks: A company advertises a product or service as a "free" or "risk-free" trial, asking only for a small shipping fee or a low introductory price, which requires entering a credit or debit card number. Buried in fine print, the offer actually enrolls the shopper in a recurring "continuity plan" that starts billing the full price automatically once the trial period ends unless the customer proactively cancels. Companies make that cancellation step deliberately difficult — burying it behind phone-only cancellation lines, multi-step account menus, or unclear deadlines — so many people are charged repeatedly before they notice. Regulators have found this pattern not just among fly-by-night sites but in mainstream subscription services, where sign-up is one click but cancellation requires navigating far more steps.
redFlags: Ad emphasizes a “risk-free” trial for just the cost of shipping and handling
You must enter full credit card information just to claim something “free”
Terms and conditions about recurring billing are in small print or a separate linked page
Cancellation requires calling a phone line, multi-step account navigation, or isn't available online even though sign-up was
No clear reminder before the trial converts into a paid subscription
realExamples: In December 2025, Instacart agreed to pay $60 million in consumer refunds to settle allegations that it failed to adequately disclose that signing up for a free trial of Instacart+ would automatically enroll consumers in a paid annual subscription with limited refund options.
In December 2025, the FTC and 21 states plus Washington, D.C. filed an amended complaint against Uber over its subscription billing and cancellation practices.
In January 2026, the FTC sued JustAnswer and its CEO, alleging consumers who signed up for a low-fee trial were enrolled without consent into a higher-priced recurring monthly subscription.

The FTC has also alleged that LA Fitness made it difficult for members to cancel add-on gym services without affecting their base membership, and that Adobe used a hidden early-termination fee to trap people into paying for subscription plans.
candidate.source: Arnold & Porter, "FTC and State AGs Continue To Scrutinize Subscription Practices Amidst a Possible Click-To-Cancel Rule Revival" (Feb. 2026), https://www.arnoldporter.com/en/perspectives/advisories/2026/02/ftc-and-state-ags-continue-to-scrutinize-subscription-practices

triage.reasoning: This describes a distinct pattern (deceptive free-trial-to-recurring-billing with obstructed cancellation) not covered by existing titles like Fake Invoice & Subscription Renewal Scam (which is phone-based renewal fraud) or Fake Online Store Scam; however, the cited source is a law firm advisory about FTC/state regulatory and enforcement activity (JustAnswer, Instacart, Uber, Amazon, Chegg, LA Fitness) rather than a report specifically framing this as a 'scam' targeting consumers, so severity/urgency are inferred cautiously and the entry blurs the line between deceptive business practice and outright scam.
